passages.title: The Suitcase for One Night
paragraphs: I packed my suitcase for one night at my aunt’s house. Soon, it held three books, four games and far too many clothes. I could hardly close it. Mum asked me to imagine the visit from beginning to end. What would I actually use? I took out things I could leave at home and chose one game to share. The lighter case rolled easily beside me. At my aunt’s door, I could carry it myself. Packing well meant choosing what was necessary（必需的）, not preparing for every possibility（可能发生的事）.

passages.title: The Shirt with the Small Label
paragraphs: Before helping with the washing, I put all our clothes in one pile. Dad asked me to check the small labels inside them. Some needed cooler water or gentler washing than others. We sorted the clothes and set one delicate shirt aside. I had noticed the labels before but never read them. Their little symbols gave useful care instructions. After the wash, we hung the clothes carefully to dry. I was glad I had stopped to pay attention to something so small. The delicate（易损的） shirt kept its shape（形状）.

passages.title: The Last Slice of Melon
paragraphs: There was one large slice of melon left, and both my brother and I wanted it. I offered to cut it in half. He looked doubtful because one side seemed sweeter. Mum suggested that I cut and he choose. Suddenly, I paid much more attention to making the pieces equal. My brother chose one, and I was happy with the other. We ate beside the kitchen window, laughing at our serious expressions. A simple agreement（约定） helped us share out the fruit without another argument（争吵） about who deserved more.

passages.title: A Different Ending for the Story
paragraphs: Our teacher stopped reading just before the story ended. We each wrote what we thought would happen next. I made the missing dog return during dinner. My partner imagined it following a familiar bus home. When we shared our endings, we explained which details had given us ideas. Then the teacher read the real ending. None of us had guessed it exactly, but several clues made sense afterwards. I enjoyed hearing the different possibilities（可能性）. A good story can leave room for our own ideas while still offering clues（线索）.

passages.title: The Page with No Pictures
paragraphs: I usually chose books with colourful pictures. One afternoon, the book I wanted was already borrowed, so the librarian suggested a short story with none. At first, I missed having something to look at. Then I began imagining the narrow street, the noisy kitchen and the girl with muddy shoes. My friend read the same story, but pictured a different kitchen. We compared our ideas and laughed. The words had given us a shared starting point. Our imaginations（想象力） could fill in the rest with different details（细节）.

passages.title: The Stamp That Printed Backwards
paragraphs: In art class, we made printing stamps from thick foam. I cut out my name and glued the letters onto a small block. When I pressed it onto paper, the letters appeared backwards. My teacher asked me to compare the stamp with its print. Whatever faced the paper appeared the other way round. I made a new stamp with a simple star instead. It printed beautifully. Later, I planned another name stamp, flipping each letter and using reverse（相反的） order. This time, I knew what to watch out for before adding ink（墨水）.

passages.title: The Minutes before My Turn
paragraphs: Before giving a short talk, I kept thinking about forgetting my words. While waiting, I read my first sentence again and again. Our teacher suggested putting the card down and noticing the room. I took a slow breath and found a friendly face near the back. When my turn came, my voice shook at first, but it grew steadier. I forgot one detail and carried on. The talk did not need to be perfect. I could get through it one sentence at a time, even with nervous（紧张的） hands and a shaky（颤抖的） voice.

passages.title: The Survey with Three Choices
paragraphs: We asked classmates which fruit they preferred: apples, oranges or bananas. Bananas received the most votes. I wrote, “Bananas are everyone’s favourite fruit.” My partner stopped me. Some pupils had wanted to choose strawberries, but our question did not include them. We changed our sentence to explain that bananas were the most popular of our three choices. The results were useful, but they did not answer every possible question. Before making a claim（说法）, we needed to think about what our survey（调查） had actually asked people to choose.

passages.title: The Same Picture from Two Sides
paragraphs: Two groups sat on opposite sides of a table and drew a toy house. When we compared our pictures, they seemed to show different buildings. One group had drawn a door and two windows. The other had drawn a plain wall with one small window. We carried our drawings around the table and understood why. Nobody had invented anything. We had simply seen different sides. To describe the whole house, we needed both views. Putting together our observations（观察结果） gave us a more complete（完整的） picture than either group had alone.

passages.title: The Paper Chain across the Room
paragraphs: Our class made a paper chain for a celebration. I began cutting strips as quickly as possible, but some were too short to form strong loops. My partner suggested agreeing on a size before continuing. We used one strip as a guide and divided the jobs: cutting, joining and checking. The chain grew steadily across our desks. When we lifted it, only one loop came apart. We repaired it before hanging the chain. Working in a hurry had wasted paper. A little preparation（准备） made the whole job more efficient（高效的）.

passages.title: Where the Sugar Went
paragraphs: I stirred a spoonful of sugar into warm water until I could no longer see the grains. Had the sugar disappeared completely? Our teacher explained that it had dissolved and spread through the water in tiny particles. The sugar was still there, although the drink looked clear. We compared it with another glass containing sand. The sand did not dissolve in the same way and settled at the bottom. Clear water could contain more than our eyes revealed. I wrote down how dissolving（溶解） differs from mixing（混合） sand into water and watching it settle.

passages.title: The Jumping Rubber Band
paragraphs: I stretched a rubber band around an empty box and gently plucked it. A low sound came out, and the band looked blurred as it moved quickly. When I stopped it with my finger, the sound stopped too. Our teacher explained that the band’s vibrations（振动） made the surrounding air move. Those vibrations travelled through the air to our ears as sound. We tried different bands and listened to the changes. A simple box had become a tiny instrument. I wanted to find out how tension（张力） could change its sound.

passages.title: The Ramp with Two Surfaces
paragraphs: We rolled a toy car down a short ramp onto the floor. First, it travelled across smooth card. Then we covered the same area with rough cloth. The car stopped sooner on the cloth. We kept the starting point the same so we could compare the runs fairly. Our teacher explained that friction can slow moving objects when surfaces rub against each other. The rough cloth resisted the car’s movement more. I began to take notice of the surfaces（表面） beneath wheels and the friction（摩擦力） that affects everyday movement.

passages.title: Day and Night on the Globe
paragraphs: Our teacher darkened the classroom and shone a lamp towards a globe. The side facing the light was bright, while the other side was dark. She turned the globe slowly, and our country moved into the light, then away again. The model helped us imagine Earth turning as different places experienced day and night. The lamp stayed still during our demonstration. I had watched the sky change every evening without picturing this movement. Now I could make sense of a familiar pattern（规律） through a simple classroom model（模型）.

passages.title: The Seeds That Travelled by Air
paragraphs: On a dry afternoon, I saw fluffy（绒毛状的） seeds lift from a dandelion（蒲公英） beside the path. Each seed carried a little tuft that helped the wind move it away. Some caught in the grass, while others travelled farther than I could follow. Not every seed would grow into a plant. It needed a suitable place with the right conditions. Still, travelling could give it a chance beyond the parent plant. I watched the next breeze carry away another seed and wondered where its journey might end.

passages.title: The Fish behind the Glass
paragraphs: At an aquarium, I watched a fish opening its mouth while the covers behind its head moved. A guide explained that water passes over its gills, which take oxygen from the water. Fish need oxygen, just as we do, but most get it in a different way. I had thought the fish was simply swallowing again and again. Now its small movements meant something new. We stood back from the glass to let others see. Beneath the colourful scales, the fish’s gills（鳃） were quietly helping it breathe（呼吸）.

passages.title: The Sign Language Greeting
paragraphs: A visitor taught our class a few greetings in the sign language she used. We watched her hands and face carefully before trying them ourselves. She explained that sign languages are real languages with their own ways of forming sentences. There is more than one sign language, so signs are not the same everywhere. I had much more to learn than a few movements. When she left, we greeted her again. She smiled at our careful attempt（尝试）. A small beginning made me want to learn more about another way of communicating（交流）.

passages.title: The Old Cinema Tickets
paragraphs: While sorting a drawer, Mum found two faded cinema tickets. I expected her to throw them away, but she smiled and told me about the film. She remembered going with her sister on a rainy afternoon and sharing an enormous bag of popcorn. The paper seemed ordinary to me until I heard the story. We placed the tickets in an album and wrote a short note beneath them. Their price was no longer important. They helped Mum hold on to a memory（回忆） that had survived long after the colours began to fade（褪色）.

passages.title: The Bus Driver’s Mirror
paragraphs: From my seat near the front of a bus, I could see the driver checking a large mirror. It showed part of the space behind him. At a stop, he waited while an older passenger found a seat. Then he checked again before moving away. I had always watched the road ahead and hardly thought about what the driver needed to see inside. Driving involved more than steering. I stayed seated and kept clear of the doorway, noticing how a mirror（镜子） helped him watch the passengers as well as the traffic（车辆）.

passages.title: The Pot of Mint by the Door
paragraphs: A neighbour kept a pot of mint（薄荷） beside her kitchen door. When she made a cool drink, she picked a few leaves and washed them carefully. I asked why she grew it in a pot instead of the garden. She explained that mint can spread quickly, and a pot helps keep it within a smaller space. She gave us a small plant of our own. At home, we found a bright place for it. I looked forward to watching the fresh leaves grow and enjoying their scent（香味）.

passages.title: The Turtle’s New Name
paragraphs: A turtle decided that everyone should call him Lightning. He painted the name on a sign and carried it through the forest. “Are you faster now?” asked a rabbit. The turtle tried to hurry, but soon felt tired. Later, he found a lost snail and patiently（耐心地） helped her reach home. The snail thanked him for waiting. That evening, the turtle put his sign away. He could enjoy a funny name without proving it was true. Being himself left more room for the qualities（品质） that made him a good friend.

passages.title: The Crow and the Shiny Button
paragraphs: A crow found a shiny button and placed it in the centre of her nest. She admired it all morning. When a sparrow asked to see it, the crow spread her wings to hide it. Soon, she was too busy guarding the button to search for food or visit anyone. At last, she invited the sparrow over and showed him her treasure（珍宝）. Nothing terrible happened. He admired it and flew away. The crow relaxed. Keeping a possession（物品） had become more enjoyable when she stopped worrying about what might happen to it.

passages.title: The Two Paths to the Pond
paragraphs: Two young goats argued over which path led to the pond. One remembered passing a tall tree; the other remembered crossing a wooden bridge. They asked an older goat to settle the argument. She drew a simple plan in the dust. Both paths reached the water from different directions. The goats had each travelled only one route and assumed it was the only one. They chose the bridge path that afternoon and returned beside the tree. On the way back, they laughed about how certain they had been with so little evidence（证据） and experience（经历）.

passages.title: The Message That Sounded Cross
paragraphs: My friend sent a short message: “Bring my book tomorrow.” I thought she sounded angry. At school, I asked if I had upset（使不安） her. She looked surprised. Her bus had arrived, so she had typed quickly before putting her phone away. She had only meant to remind me. We laughed, but I remembered how easily I had added a tone that was not there. Written words do not always show someone’s mood（情绪）. Now I check with the person before turning a short message into a bigger problem.

passages.title: The Practice Nobody Saw
paragraphs: My classmate played a short piano piece at assembly. It sounded easy when she performed it. Later, I visited her home and saw a notebook filled with practice dates. She showed me one difficult bar and played it slowly several times. I had seen only the finished performance, not the patient work behind it. That afternoon, I practised my own recorder without rushing through the tricky notes. Getting better at something could happen quietly, long before an audience noticed. Her progress（进步） had grown from small, repeated efforts（努力）.

passages.title: The Drawing I Was Allowed to Refuse
paragraphs: A classmate asked me to draw pictures for her project because she liked my artwork. I wanted to help, but I already had homework and a family visit that evening. I nearly agreed, although I knew I would struggle. Instead, I explained that I could suggest ideas during break but could not finish the drawings for her. She accepted my offer and began sketching herself. Being helpful did not mean agreeing to everything. I could say no to a request politely while still showing kindness（友善） and respect（尊重）.

passages.title: The Group Chat after Bedtime
paragraphs: Our class project group kept sending messages late one evening. I wanted to answer every idea, but I was ready for bed. The next morning, several classmates said they had felt the same. We agreed on a time to stop messaging and kept important decisions in one short note. Anyone who missed the evening discussion could read it later. The project continued smoothly, and nobody needed to stay awake for every message. Setting aside time to rest helped us return with more energy（精力） and better concentration（专注力）.

passages.title: The Question I Saved for Later
paragraphs: During a science lesson, I suddenly wondered how astronauts（宇航员） wash their clothes. It was an interesting question, but our teacher was explaining something else. I wrote it in the margin（页边空白） of my notebook instead of interrupting. At the end, I asked whether we could explore it another day. She suggested bringing it to our next question session. Writing it down meant I did not have to forget it or stop listening. I could come back to a new idea when there was time to give it proper attention（关注）.

passages.title: A Collection with a Limit
paragraphs: I loved collecting smooth pebbles on walks, and soon my shelf was crowded. I could hardly see my favourite ones. Mum gave me a small tray and suggested keeping only what fitted inside. Choosing was harder than finding more stones. I kept a striped pebble, a flat grey one and several with unusual shapes. The rest went into our garden. With fewer objects, I noticed each one more clearly. A limit（限制） did not spoil my hobby. It helped me make room for the things I valued most in my collection（收藏品）.

passages.title: The Things We Could Not Measure
paragraphs: For a maths activity, we measured the length of our classroom and counted its chairs. Then our teacher asked us to describe the room using no numbers. We mentioned the cheerful noise before lessons, the smell of new books and the feeling of belonging. None of these fitted neatly on our measuring tape. Numbers helped explain the size of the room, but our descriptions added something else. We needed both to build up a fuller picture. I wrote “a place where I feel welcome” beneath our measurements（测量结果） and calculations（计算）.
